paragraphs.source_en: Another important analogy in the archaeological record of the northern Niger is the presence of pottery associated with the Early Holocene hunter-gatherers. At Temet I in the Adrar Bous, beside stone vessels, a comb for pottery decoration was found in a layer dating to 9,550+100 BP (calBP10, 902±169) and also two sherds probably belonging to this sequence (Barich 1998a) were also found. At Tagalagal in the Air the pottery dated to 9,370+130 BP (calBP 10,637±216) consists of various shapes, excellent quality and already displayed the whole range of decorated motifs, indicating that the technique and production were already firmly established (Roset 1983). At Gobero cemetery ceramics with dotted wavy-lines and zigzag impressed motifs were found in the burial fill, in an associated refuse area and in nearby palaeo-lake deposits of the Early Holocene phase (Sereno et al. 2008).

paragraphs.source_en: In other Saharan regions the pottery seems to be younger. In the neighbouring mountains of Tibesti ceramics with dotted wavy-line decorations were dated to 8,065+100 BP (calBP 8,949±169) (Beltrami 2007). In the Eastern Sahara, the early dating of pottery at 9,330+110 BP (calBP 10,534±155) at Khartoum in Sudan is considered to be unreliable and the oldest securely dated ceramics are at 8,640+120 BP (calBP 9,710±158) (Elamin & Mohammed-Ali 2004). In the northern Sahara the pottery appears only in the 8th millennium BP (Chavaillon 1992). The nucleus of the oldest Saharan pottery appears therefore to be the southern Tassili in Algeria and the Air and Adrar Bous mountains in Niger. Since an older pottery has not been found anywhere in Africa so far, this is the most likely location for the high-fired ceramics from which this technique spread into other regions.

paragraphs.source_en: The carefully executed impressed decoration on the vessels testifies to the aesthetic perception of the hunter-gatherers. As mentioned earlier, in the Tassili, pottery decoration is similar to the body decoration of the Round Head figures. This fact cannot be applied to the Air and Adrar Bous mountains because to date no Round Head paintings have been found in those areas. However, the pottery in this area is an indicator of an economic and cultural transformation occurring at the beginning of the Early Holocene. If the pottery decoration is related to the Round Head body decoration, it is plausible that origins of these paintings are related to the areas where the earliest ceramics were found, and the Round Heads may have started to appear as soon as the first high-fired ceramics.
